Lesson 01

Introduction to Robotics

What a robot is, how it thinks, and what it's made of.

01
Lesson 1. Here you will learn what makes a machine a robot, the loop every robot follows, and the parts that every robot is built from.
1.1 What is a robot?

A machine that senses, decides and acts

A robot is a machine that can sense its surroundings, decide what to do using a program, and act on the physical world, with some degree of independence from a human operator.
Home

Robot vacuum

Maps a living room as it cleans.

Factory

Six-axis arm

Welds car bodies all day.

Campus

Delivery robot

Moves through university corridors.

Reception

Humanoid

Greets visitors and answers questions.

A robot is a machine that can sense its surroundings, decide what to do using a program, and act on the physical world, with some independence from a human. Look at the four examples. Each one senses, decides and acts in its own setting.
1.1 Robotics

Robotics brings four fields together

  • Mechanical engineering gives the robot its body.
  • Electronics gives it sensors, power and control circuits.
  • Computer science gives it software and intelligence.
  • Mathematics ties them together through geometry, kinematics and control theory.
Robotics is the engineering field that designs, builds, programs and operates robots. It brings together mechanical engineering for the body, electronics for sensors and power, computer science for software and intelligence, and mathematics for geometry, kinematics and control. That is why your programme covers all four.
1.2 The sense–think–act model

Every robot runs the same loop, many times a second

Sense: sensors

Turn distance, light, tilt, sound or touch into electrical signals.

Think: controller

A program turns readings into decisions, from one if–else up to a large AI model.

Act: actuators

Motors, servos, grippers, speakers and lights carry out the decision.

Every robot repeats the same loop many times every second. It senses, using sensors. It thinks, using a controller running a program. It acts, using actuators like motors. Then it senses the result of its own action and starts again. Watch the yellow dot travel around the loop.
1.2 Two everyday loops

A person and a robot vacuum think the same way

StepTouching a hot panRobot vacuum hits a wall
SenseSkin senses heatBump sensor detects the wall
ThinkBrain decides it is dangerousController decides to turn
ActArm muscles pull the hand awayWheel motors change direction
You already use this loop yourself. When you touch a hot pan, your skin senses heat, your brain decides it is dangerous, and your muscles pull your hand away. A robot vacuum does the same with a bump sensor, a controller and wheel motors.
1.3 Robot, automation or remote control?

Tap each machine: is it a robot?

If any of the three steps is missing, or a human does the thinking, it is automation or teleoperation.

Not every machine with a motor is a robot. If one of the three steps is missing, or a human does the thinking, it is automation or teleoperation instead. Tap each card to check whether you guessed right.
1.3 Levels of autonomy

From joystick to fully on its own

Teleoperatedhuman
Semi-autonomousshared
Fully autonomousrobot

A teleoperated robot is driven by a person in real time.

A semi-autonomous robot handles some tasks itself (such as balancing) while a person gives high-level commands.

A fully autonomous robot plans and carries out its task on its own.

Sirena example: UBot is both autonomous and semi-autonomous. It can be driven from a mobile app, or carry out tasks with less supervision.
Robots differ in how much of the thinking they do themselves. A teleoperated robot is driven by a person in real time. A semi-autonomous robot handles some tasks itself. A fully autonomous robot plans and carries out its task on its own. Sirena's UBot can work in both semi-autonomous and autonomous ways.
1.4 Main components of a robot

Six building blocks around a controller

🧠 Controller

The brain: a microcontroller, an SBC, or both.

👁 Sensors

Measure the world and the robot's own state.

💪 Actuators

The muscles: create motion or output.

🔋 Power supply

Batteries, chargers, voltage regulators.

🦿 Mechanical body

Frame, links, joints, wheels or legs.

📡 Software & comms

Programs, AI, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB, serial.

Almost every robot is built from six blocks around a controller: the controller, sensors, actuators, a power supply, a mechanical body, and software with communication links. Press Next to reveal each block and its role.
1.5 Sensors at a glance

Proprioceptive (the robot itself) vs exteroceptive (the world)

SensorMeasuresExampleRobot useType
Distance (ultrasonic, IR, LiDAR)How far an object isHC-SR04, Sharp IRObstacles, mappingextero
IMUAcceleration, rotation, headingMPU-9250 (in NINO)Balance, tiltproprio
EncoderWheel or joint rotationOptical / magneticOdometry, joint positionproprio
CameraImages and videoUSB or CSI cameraDetection, navigationextero
Touch / forceContact, pressureCapacitive pad, bumperInteraction, collisionsextero
MicrophoneSoundMicrophone arrayVoice commandsextero
EnvironmentalTemperature, humidity, gas, lightDHT11, LDRMonitoringextero
Sensors come in two groups. Proprioceptive sensors measure the robot itself, like an IMU or an encoder. Exteroceptive sensors measure the outside world, like distance sensors, cameras and microphones. When you choose a sensor, think about its range, resolution, update rate and when it fails.
1.5 Actuators at a glance

How robots move

DC motor

Spins continuously; speed set by PWM. Used for wheels.

Hobby servo

Moves to and holds an angle. Small quadruped legs.

Smart servo

Angle plus feedback of position, load and temperature. NINO uses Dynamixel.

Stepper

Moves in exact fixed steps. 3D printers, CNC.

Pneumatic / hydraulic

Air or fluid pushes a piston. Very high force.

Actuators are how robots move. Watch each animation. A DC motor spins continuously. A hobby servo moves to an angle and holds it. A smart servo also reports position, load and temperature. A stepper moves in exact steps. Pneumatic and hydraulic actuators push a piston with very high force.
1.6 Degrees of freedom

One DOF = one independent way to move

Two-wheeled robot (plane)3
Industrial arm6
Perro quadruped12
Twist multi-legged12
NINO humanoid20

More DOF = more flexibility, but heavier, costlier and harder to control.

A degree of freedom is one independent way a robot can move. Each motorised joint usually adds one. The animated arm has three joints, so three degrees of freedom. An industrial arm has six, Perro and Twist have twelve, and NINO has twenty. More freedom means more flexibility, but more cost and harder control.
1.7 Why do we build robots?

Where robots beat people: the three Ds

Dull

Highly repetitive work.

Dirty

Unpleasant or unhygienic work.

Dangerous

Toxic, hot, heavy or remote work.

Robots also add value where these matter:

Precision

Electronics assembly, surgery.

Scale

Warehouses shipping millions of orders.

Interaction & learning

Education and customer service: Sirena's focus.

Robots are used for work that is dull, dirty or dangerous. They also help where precision, scale, or interaction and learning matter. Interaction and learning is the main focus of Sirena's robots.

Lesson 02

History of Robotics

A story of bottlenecks removed, one at a time.

02
Lesson 2. The history of robotics is a story of problems solved one at a time. Knowing it explains why robots look the way they do today.
The big picture

Each era solved the next hardest problem

1st

Actuation

How to move precisely

2nd

Computing

How to decide

3rd

Sensing

How to perceive

Now

Intelligence & balance

How to adapt and walk

This explains why robots look the way they do today, and why legged and humanoid robots arrived only recently.

First, engineers solved actuation: how to move precisely. Then computing: how to decide. Then sensing: how to perceive. Today they are solving intelligence and balance: how to adapt and walk.
2.1 From myths and automata to "robot"

Before real robots: stories and clockwork

Centuries ago

Automata

Clockwork figures that wrote, played music or imitated animals. Fixed sequence, no sensing, so not robots.

1920

R.U.R.

Karel Čapek's play introduces "robot", from the Czech robota: forced labour.

1942

Three Laws

Isaac Asimov's Runaround. He is also credited with coining "robotics". His laws framed robot safety as a design problem.

For centuries, inventors built clockwork automata, but these followed a fixed sequence and could not sense, so they were not robots. The word robot comes from Karel Capek's 1920 play R.U.R., from the Czech word for forced labour. In 1942, Isaac Asimov wrote the Three Laws of Robotics.
2.2 The industrial era

Modern robotics began in the factory

1961

Unimate

Devol & Engelberger (Unimation). At General Motors, it lifted and stacked hot die-cast parts: dull, dirty and dangerous.

1969

Stanford Arm

All-electric and computer-controlled; the model for later designs.

1973

KUKA Famulus

Among the first with six electromechanically driven axes.

1978

PUMA

Programmable Universal Machine for Assembly: brought robots into assembly work.

That is why industrial arms are still the largest single category of robots.

Modern robotics began in factories. Unimate started work at General Motors in 1961, lifting hot metal parts, a dull, dirty and dangerous job. The Stanford Arm, the KUKA Famulus and PUMA followed. That is why industrial arms are still the biggest category of robots.
2.3 Mobile and intelligent robots

Leaving the cell needed sensing and onboard computing

1966

Shakey

SRI. First mobile robot to reason about its own actions.

1997

Sojourner

NASA rover explores Mars.

2002

Roomba

An affordable robot in homes.

2005

Stanley

Wins the DARPA desert race after no vehicle finished in 2004.

2007

ROS

Work begins on the Robot Operating System.

2012

Kiva

Amazon buys Kiva; mobile robots drive warehouses.

To leave the factory, robots needed sensing and onboard computing. Shakey was the first mobile robot to reason about its actions. Sojourner explored Mars, Roomba entered homes, Stanley won the DARPA desert race, ROS gave robots shared software, and Kiva robots transformed warehouses.
2.4 The legged and humanoid era

Walking is harder than rolling

1973

WABOT-1

Waseda University. First full-scale humanoid.

2000

ASIMO

Honda shows smooth humanoid walking.

2005

BigDog

A quadruped balancing on rough ground.

2020

Spot

Goes on commercial sale.

2024

Electric Atlas

Plus a wave of humanoid start-ups.

India

NINO

Described by Sirena as the first intelligent humanoid built by an Indian company.

Enablers: lighter, stronger motors · lithium batteries · low-cost IMUs · fast embedded processors · learned control and AI.

Walking is much harder than rolling, because the robot must keep its balance all the time. WABOT-1, ASIMO, BigDog, Spot and the electric Atlas show how legged robots developed. In India, Sirena built NINO, an intelligent humanoid for education.
2.5 What history teaches

Three eras that now work side by side

EraBottleneck removedEnabling technologyExample robots
Industrial 1960s–80sPrecise, repeatable motionElectric & hydraulic actuators, early computersUnimate, Stanford Arm, PUMA
Mobile & service 1990s–2010sSensing and onboard decisionsCheap sensors, MCUs, batteries, ROSSojourner, Roomba, Stanley, Kiva
Legged & humanoid 2000s–todayDynamic balance and interactionIMUs, smart servos, embedded AI, lithium batteriesASIMO, Spot, Atlas, NINO
This table sums up the three eras: industrial, mobile and service, and legged and humanoid. Notice that no era replaced the one before. All three kinds of robot work side by side today.

Lesson 03

Types of Microcontrollers

The chips and computers that act as a robot's brain.

03
Lesson 3. Here you will meet the chips and computers that act as a robot's brain.
3.1 What is a microcontroller?

A complete small computer on one chip

Processor core + flash + RAM + built-in peripherals: GPIO, ADC, timers and communication interfaces.

Cheap

Everything on one chip.

Low power

Runs on batteries for a long time.

Instant start

No operating system to boot.

Microsecond reaction

Ideal for the "think" step next to sensors and motors.

A microcontroller is a complete small computer on one chip. It has a processor, flash memory, RAM, and peripherals such as input-output pins, an analogue to digital converter, and timers. It is cheap, low power, starts instantly and reacts in microseconds.
3.2 Key building blocks and terms

Tap a card to flip it

Watch the voltage: classic boards use 5 V logic; most modern chips use 3.3 V. Mixing them without care can damage components.
Tap each red card to flip it and learn a key term. When you have read all eight, note the warning below: many classic boards use 5 volt logic, but modern chips use 3.3 volts. Mixing them carelessly can damage parts.
3.3 MCU, MPU or SBC?

Three kinds of brain

FeatureMicrocontroller (MCU)Microprocessor (MPU)Single-board computer (SBC)
What it isCPU, memory, I/O on one chipCPU only; needs external chipsFull computer on one board
OSUsually none (bare-metal)Linux, WindowsLinux or similar
TimingVery predictable, µsDepends on OSNot real-time
Power & costVery lowHigherModerate
Robot roleMotor control, sensorsLaptops, serversVision, planning, networking, apps
ExampleArduino Uno, ESP32Intel, AMDRaspberry Pi
A microcontroller runs one program without an operating system and has very predictable timing. A microprocessor is only a CPU and needs other chips. A single-board computer, like a Raspberry Pi, is a full computer running Linux. Robots use microcontrollers for motors and sensors, and single-board computers for vision and planning.
3.4 Popular microcontroller families

The boards you'll meet again and again

Family (board)Core & clockMemoryStrengthsTypical use
AVR Arduino Uno8-bit · 16 MHz32 KB flash · 2 KB RAMSimplest, huge communityBeginner robots
AVR Arduino Mega8-bit · 16 MHz256 KB flash · 8 KB RAMMany I/O pinsMany sensors & motors
ESP3232-bit dual · 240 MHz~520 KB RAMWi-Fi + Bluetooth, low costApp-controlled, IoT
STM32ARM Cortex-M0…M7Wide rangeIndustrial grade, precise timersMotor drivers, drones
RP2040 Picodual M0+ · 133 MHz264 KB RAMVery low cost, PIOServo, LED, education
PIC8 / 16 / 32-bitWide rangeLong history, low powerAppliances, industry
These are the families you will meet most often. The Arduino Uno is the simplest to learn. The Mega has many pins. The ESP32 adds Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. The STM32 is industrial grade. The RP2040 is very low cost. PIC chips have a long industry history.
3.5 SBCs and edge-AI modules

Modern robots stack their brains

Microcontroller

Fast, time-critical reflexes: motors, sensors.

Single-board computer

Planning, maps, networking, apps.

Edge-AI module

Runs neural networks on the robot.

Edge AI runs AI models on the robot, not in a remote cloud: faster responses, works offline, keeps camera data private.
Modern robots stack their brains in layers. A microcontroller handles fast reflexes. A single-board computer handles planning and networking. An edge AI module runs neural networks right on the robot, which is faster, works offline and keeps camera data private.
3.6 How to choose a controller

A real engineering decision

  • Task complexity: blinking lights → 8-bit MCU; camera navigation → SBC or edge AI.
  • Number of I/O: count sensors, motors and servos.
  • Connectivity: app control → ESP32 or SBC with Wi-Fi.
  • Timing: precise motor control → MCU hardware timers.
  • Power budget: performance vs battery run time.
  • Cost & ecosystem: community, documentation, libraries.
Example: weighted decision matrix

App-controlled delivery robot, no camera. Weighted totals (example scores):

Arduino Uno87
ESP3298
Raspberry Pi79

Each criterion gets a weight; each board a score. The highest total wins, and the choice is easy to defend.

Choosing a controller is a real engineering decision. Think about task complexity, number of inputs and outputs, connectivity, timing, power and cost. Engineers use a weighted decision matrix to compare boards fairly. In this example, the ESP32 wins for an app-controlled robot without a camera.

Lesson 04

Types of Robots

Wheeled, legged, humanoid and industrial.

04
Lesson 4. Here you will learn the main robot families: wheeled, legged, humanoid and industrial.
Classifying robots

Three ways to sort a robot

How it moves

Fixed · wheeled · legged · flying · swimming

Where it works

Factory · warehouse · home · hospital · outdoors

What it does

Manipulation · transport · inspection · interaction

This lesson uses the most common beginner classification: body plan.

Robots can be sorted by how they move, where they work, or what they do. In this lesson we sort them by body plan.
4.1 Wheeled robots

Simple, efficient, naturally stable

Equal speeds: straight

Wheels struggle with stairs, gaps and rough ground. The drive configuration decides how the robot moves and turns.

Differential drive

Two driven wheels + caster. Equal speeds go straight, unequal speeds turn, opposite speeds spin on the spot.

Sirena's UBot is a wheeled robot with an indoor base built for stable, precise movement.

Wheeled robots are simple, efficient and stable, but they struggle with stairs and rough ground. Watch the differential drive robot. Equal wheel speeds drive it straight. Unequal speeds make it curve. Opposite speeds spin it on the spot.
4.1 Drive configurations

Four common ways to arrange wheels

Differential

Two wheels + caster. Most common indoors.

Ackermann

Car-like steering. Stable at speed, but can't turn on the spot.

Omni / mecanum

Rollers let it slide sideways. Good for tight aisles.

Tracked

Tracks grip rough ground. Inspection and defence.

There are four common wheel arrangements. Differential drive is most common indoors. Ackermann steering works like a car. Omni and mecanum wheels can slide sideways. Tracks grip rough ground.
4.2 Legged robots

Legs cross what wheels can't, but must balance

Support polygon: the ground area enclosed by the feet that are down. The robot is statically stable while its centre of mass (orange) stays above it.

Quadruped crawl: one leg up, still stable. Trot: two diagonal legs up, only dynamically stable. Hexapod tripod gait: three feet always down, so always stable.

Legged robots can cross ground that stops wheels, but they must balance. The support polygon is the area between the feet on the ground. A robot is statically stable while its centre of mass, shown in orange, stays above that area. Watch how lifting legs changes the shape.
4.2 Programming small legged robots

Keyframes: poses played in sequence

Each keyframe stores a target angle for every joint motor. The controller moves smoothly from one pose to the next.

This is exactly how custom actions are recorded on Sirena's Perro and Twist.

Small legged robots are often programmed with keyframes. Each keyframe stores an angle for every motor, and the robot moves smoothly from one pose to the next. Watch the leg play its frames. This is how actions are recorded on Perro and Twist.
4.3 Humanoid robots

Built for human spaces and human interaction

Legs

Walking and balance.

Arms & hands

Gestures, manipulation.

Head

Cameras, mics, speakers.

Interaction layer

Displays, touch, voice.

ZMP (Zero Moment Point): keep the point where the ground pushes back inside the foot's support area, and the robot won't tip.
A humanoid has a head, torso, two arms and usually two legs, so it can work in spaces made for people. Walking humanoids stay balanced using the Zero Moment Point principle, keeping the ground's push inside the foot's support area.
4.4 Industrial robots

Programmable arms bolted in place

Articulated

Rotary joints, usually 6 DOF. Most flexible.

SCARA

Fast flat assembly: placing parts, screws.

Delta

Three light arms. Super-fast pick-and-place.

Cartesian

Straight X/Y/Z. 3D printers, CNC.

Judged by payload · reach · repeatability · speed

Industrial robots are programmable arms fixed in place. Articulated arms are the most flexible, SCARA robots are fast at flat assembly, delta robots are fastest at pick and place, and Cartesian robots move along straight axes. They are judged by payload, reach, repeatability and speed.
4.4 Collaborative robots

Cobots work beside people, without cages

Limit speed & force

Safe enough to share a workspace.

Stop on contact

They detect a bump and halt.

Affordable automation

Opens robotics to small and medium factories.

Coming later: the tool position of an arm is calculated from its joint angles by forward kinematics.
Collaborative robots, or cobots, work safely beside people without cages. They limit their speed and force and stop when they touch something, which makes automation affordable for small factories.

4.6 Other robot types

Beyond the big four

Aerial

Drones for inspection, mapping, delivery.

Underwater

Pipeline and ship-hull inspection.

Space

Rovers. Chandrayaan-3 landed Pragyan on the Moon in 2023.

Soft

Flexible materials for safe gripping.

Swarm

There are other robot types too: aerial drones, underwater robots, space rovers, soft robots and swarms. India's Chandrayaan-3 mission landed the Pragyan rover on the Moon in 2023.

Lesson 5. Here you will see how the robotics industry is organised, and the careers it offers.
5.1 How the industry is organised

The robotics value chain

Each stage adds value before a robot does useful work, and engineers can build careers at every stage.

RaaS (robots-as-a-service): customers rent robots with service contracts instead of buying them.
The robotics industry is a value chain. Component makers supply parts. Robot makers build platforms. Software and AI companies provide the brains. System integrators install complete solutions. End users operate the robots, sometimes renting them as a service.
5.2 Market segments

Different markets, different skills

0

new industrial robots installed worldwide each year in recent years: more than half a million, according to the IFR's World Robotics reports.

Asia, led by China, is the largest market. Education and research (highlighted in the figure) is Sirena's core segment.

Robots are sold into very different markets. The International Federation of Robotics reports more than half a million new industrial robots installed worldwide each year in recent years. Education and research is Sirena's core segment.

Six forces shaping robotics now

Humanoid pilots

Humanoids are moving from demos into factory and warehouse trials.

AI foundation models

03

Six trends are shaping robotics: humanoids moving into pilot projects, AI foundation models, edge AI, cobots and robots as a service, simulation-first development, and stronger safety standards.
5.5 Robotics in India

Growing on five fronts

Manufacturing

Automotive and electronics automation.

Warehousing

Start-ups like Bengaluru's Ati Motors.

Space

India's robotics sector is growing in manufacturing, warehousing, industrial vehicles, space and education. Government support for local manufacturing means more demand for engineers who can install, program and maintain robots.

MCB on/off; UART/HDMI for PC configuration
Blinking green: ready to connectSolid green: app connectedRed: low battery or error
UBot is a utility robot that carries items around campuses, and it has been used at Shoolini University. A Raspberry Pi is its brain, and you drive it with an Android app over Wi-Fi. Watch its status light: blinking green means ready, solid green means connected, and red means low battery or an error.
6.4 NINO · Humanoid

The flagship: robotics meets conversational AI

Size
53.6 cm tall, about 3 kg
Controller
NINO Module CPU (Sirena's in-house processor) + I/O & power board; Linux-derived OS
Actuators
20 Dynamixel smart servos: MX-28 (M1–M12), AX-18 (M13–M20)
Sensors
Touch (head), IR distance 4–50 cm (chest), 9-axis IMU (torso)
Vision & audio
HD camera, 3 far-field mics, 2 speakers, 2 LCD displays
Power
2 × Li-ion packs, 3,400 mAh each
Connectivity
Wi-Fi, USB
Software
Sirena Studio, Android, Python, C#, MATLAB, V-REP
NINO is Sirena's flagship humanoid. It is 53.6 centimetres tall, with 20 smart servos, a camera, three microphones, two speakers, an IMU for balance, an IR distance sensor and a touch sensor. It responds to a spoken hot-word and can talk back.
6.4 NINO · Programming

Designing actions on a computer

  • Brings together almost every concept in this module: actuators, sensors, embedded computing, balance and AI.
  • Designed for education, research and human–robot interaction.
  • Later modules use NINO for computer vision, generative AI and reinforcement learning.
NINO brings together almost every topic in this module: actuators, sensors, embedded computing, balance and AI. You program its actions from a computer, and later modules use it for computer vision and AI.
6.5 Perro · Quadruped

12 servos, three per leg

Postures

Sit, Stand and Neutral with a single tap.

Movement

Walk in four directions, 90° turns, body tilt, adjustable speed.

Camera feed

A USB camera streams a live view to the app.

Action recording

Frames store an angle for every motor: the keyframe method.

Perro is a four-legged robot with twelve servos, three per leg. It can sit, stand, walk, turn and tilt, stream video from a USB camera, and record actions as keyframes.
6.6 Twist · Multi-legged

A spider robot for stable walking and motion design

12 motors and a library of actions: wakeup, greet, happy, yoga, walking stance.

Group control

One angle applied to several motors for symmetric moves.

Frame editing

Reorder frames by drag-and-drop; save, load, replay.

With many legs on the ground, Twist is ideal for studying static stability and gait design.

Twist is a multi-legged spider robot with twelve motors and ready-made actions like greet and yoga. Its app lets you control groups of motors and edit frames, which makes it great for learning about stability and gait design.
6.7 Biped and humanoid platforms

The hardest problem: walking on two legs

Biped

Small support area, so active balance

Teaches leg kinematics, gait cycles, centre-of-mass control and the ZMP principle, before full humanoids.

Humanoid platforms

Led by NINO

Legs, arms, head sensors and AI in one system. Used in advanced modules on humanoid design, DOF, kinematics, power and electronics, and AI interaction.

Exact configurations of the biped and larger humanoid research platforms are in Sirena's platform documentation.

The biped platform teaches the hardest problem: walking on two legs with active balance. The humanoid platforms, led by NINO, combine legs, arms, sensors and AI for advanced study.

7.1 Key takeaways

Seven things to remember

  • A robot senses, thinks and acts with some independence. Human thinking = teleoperation; fixed sequence = automation.
  • Six blocks: controller, sensors, actuators, power, body, software & comms.
  • History removed bottlenecks in actuation, computing, sensing and balance.
  • MCU = fast, low-power control · SBC = planning and networking · edge AI = neural networks on the robot.
  • Wheels for flat floors, legs for rough terrain, humanoids for human spaces, arms for precision.
  • Value chain: components → robot makers → software → integrators → end users, with growing roles in India.
  • Sirena's ecosystem lets you study every robot family on real hardware.
Here are the seven key takeaways from this module. Try to say each one in your own words before you press Next to reveal it.
